agent_notes: The superscription 'of David, a psalm' is verse 1 in the Hebrew (KJV 101:0); the verse map handles it. 'Of David' (ledavid) is read as attribution, not dedication; the lamed is ambiguous and I kept the neutral 'of David'.

Rashi and the Talmud (Berakhot 60b, as cited by Meiri) read 'chesed and mishpat' as two modes of divine action to be praised alike; Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri read them as the king's own conduct. The Hebrew allows both; the translations keep the ambiguity, and the commentary states the royal reading as primary because the rest of the psalm is the king's program.

agent_notes: Revised per the reviewer request: the commentary no longer says the KJV 'cut off' softens atzmit. It says the verb means to put an end to, and that Metzudat Zion, Metzudat David and Meiri gloss it with karat, so the KJV is accurate; the link to verse 8 is kept. The recurrence of the verb in verse 8 is my own observation from the Hebrew, outside this window; the sense rests on Metzudat Zion's cross-reference to Psalm 94.

The final אוּכָל has no object word beyond אֹתוֹ and no verb complement. The commentators split: Rashi 'that he be my companion', Radak and Ibn Ezra 'I cannot see him / bear him', Metzudat David 'cannot endure'. I kept the literal 'I am not able' with the bracketed 'to endure' as the least committal rendering, and the dramatic layer follows 'endure' (also YLT and KJV's 'suffer'). The Ibn Ezra comment about 'wide of heart' meaning a wise man whom the king cannot cut off is a different reading; I mention it but do not adopt it.

מְלָשְׁנִי is marked Q(k) in the packet: the packet's form carries an extra yod, which Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat Zion all call superfluous (yod yetera). I glossed the participle 'one who slanders' without further claims about the Ketiv.

Malbim reads 'faithful to the land' as against Near Eastern rulers who chose advisers loyal only to the ruler; this is his reading, and I cite it as such in the commentary rather than asserting it.

agent_notes: 'Cut off from the city of YHWH' is taken, with Radak, Meiri and the Targum, to mean Jerusalem; the text only says 'city of YHWH'. The dramatic layer says 'the city of the LORD' and leaves Jerusalem to the commentary.

'Labbekarim' ('to the mornings') is literal 'at the mornings'; the English versions split between 'early' (KJV, a misreading of the idiom) and 'morning by morning' (ASV). I chose the latter in the dramatic layer and a literal 'to the mornings' in the literal layer.
